name: Croatian Sign Language
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Sign language; word stress category inapplicable and no prosodic-stress description located

new_statements.quote: Malaia, Wilbur, and Milković (2013) introduced another calculated measure, the Ratio of the Telic-Atelic Slopes, as an indication of how fast the movement comes to a stop (Maximum deceleration) in the two types of signs. In both ASL and HZJ, the slope for telics is greater than for atelics. A comparison of the Ratios reveals that HZJ telic slopes are nearly twice those of atelics whereas for ASL the difference is much smaller. This shows that in HZJ deceleration may be secondary to peak velocity, which indicates that a further study of HZJ stress marking is needed. [p. 151, fn. 17] ... No sign language has been observed to have distinctive lexical stress, comparable to English 'permit (noun) and per'mit (verb) (Jantunen and Takkinen, 2010). [p. 151]
new_statements.citation: Wilbur, Ronnie B. (2022). Prosody in Sign Languages. Hrvatska revija za rehabilitacijska istraživanja 58 (Special Issue), 143-174. doi:10.31299/hrri.58.si.8
new_statements.locator: fn. 17, p. 151 (PDF p. 9); general sign-stress statements §2.5-2.6, pp. 149-151
new_statements.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states where stress falls in HZJ. Wilbur (2022), writing as the PI of the HZJ grammar project, says explicitly that HZJ stress marking still needs to be studied; the only HZJ data are kinematic (telic vs atelic verb deceleration, Malaia et al. 2013). Her cross-sign-language generalization is that sign stress is realized by movement kinematics (peak velocity; duration marks phrase position), that no sign language has contrastive lexical stress, and that in ASL lexical stress is predictable on the first (usually only) syllable - but this is stated for ASL/sign languages generally, not for HZJ.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described for HZJ. Wilbur 2022 p. 151 (ASL): reduplicated noun forms have prominence on the first syllable only; monomorphemic disyllables (BABY, CANCEL type) have equal prominence on both syllables; compounds have the second syllable stronger.
new_statements.exceptions: None for HZJ. For ASL: lexical disyllables with equal prominence and compounds with final prominence are the exceptions to first-syllable stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Wilbur's discussion is about sign-level (lexical) stress vs phrase position within sentences; sign languages have no F0, so prominence is cued by velocity/displacement/duration. The HZJ remark concerns single signs (verbs) in a motion-capture study, not citation forms in a wordlist.
new_statements.identity_note: Sign language (Glottolog family 'Sign Language', ISO csq), used in Croatia; NSF grammar project data are Zagreb signers. Word stress in the spoken-language sense is inapplicable; 'stress' here means sign-level prominence cued by movement kinematics. No dialect distinction made in any source seen.

sources.note: Review of sign-language prosody by the PI of the HZJ grammar project; §2.5-2.6 (pp. 149-151) say sign stress is marked by movement kinematics (peak velocity), that no sign language has distinctive lexical stress and ASL stress is predictable on the first syllable; the only HZJ-specific remark is fn. 17, p. 151: HZJ telic/atelic deceleration ratios differ from ASL, 'which indicates that a further study of HZJ stress marking is needed' - i.e. HZJ stress marking is explicitly unstudied.
